Caching Strategies for Web Services

By Jordan Lee, March 3, 2026

Caching is the cheapest way to make a service faster, but it is also an easy way to serve stale data. This article compares the common approaches and shows how to pick between them. For a longer treatment see the full caching guide, and for background on HTTP semantics read HTTP basics.

Choosing a strategy

The right strategy depends on how often the data changes, how costly a miss is, and how much staleness your users will tolerate. Start by measuring your hit ratio before you add any complexity, because many services find that a small time-to-live on a single layer is all they need.

  • Cache-aside keeps the application in control of reads and writes.
  • Write-through updates the cache and the store together.
  • Write-behind batches writes for throughput at the cost of durability.

Comparison

StrategyRead latencyDurability
Cache-asideLowHigh
Write-throughLowHigh
Write-behindLowestMedium

Example

A minimal cache-aside lookup looks like this. Notice that the cache is only populated on a miss, which keeps rarely used keys out of memory.

def get_user(user_id):
    cached = cache.get(user_id)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    user = db.load(user_id)
    cache.set(user_id, user, ttl=60)
    return user

Finally, remember to monitor evictions. A cache that evicts constantly is a cache that is too small, and no amount of clever invalidation will fix that.
